vignette:
Raúl Mendez had been working late in his apartment office in Houston when the memory that still governs his days first took shape. Years ago, after a traffic stop that turned violent, police officers had forced him against a cruiser, wrenched his arm up behind him, and kept him on the pavement while his face scraped the concrete. He remembers the sting of that pain most vividly, the smell of hot asphalt, and the sight of his own blood and bruised knuckles while strangers stood nearby and watched. What unsettles Raúl now is how readily his mind returns to the parts that looked like injury in that moment: a split lip on a man in a convenience store line, a cut on a coworker's forearm, the raw swelling around a stranger's eye. Each of those reminders does more than stir the memory; it immediately pushes Raúl into the same judgment that the world is marked by injury and that he cannot trust what he is seeing. Once a bruise or cut catches his eye, he is convinced danger is already present and that he is the kind of person who will miss it until it is too late. Those sights land in him with the force of proof that danger is already present, and he immediately feels set apart from other people, as if he is the only one living with an event that changed the way he sees the world. In those moments he has come to believe that there is something about him that made it happen, that he must have done something wrong, and the same thought spills into a darker place where he is not sure his life is worth living anymore.

After the arrest, Raúl's days began to narrow around caution. He no longer trusts unfamiliar places, because he cannot assess the danger there and feels foolish for not knowing where the exits are, who is watching, or whether a situation can turn on him without warning. Living that way has made the whole city feel salted with warnings to him, so that a glare through a storefront window, a doorway left half open, or a raised voice in a hallway can suddenly become a reminder of what he assumes is waiting around him. The more threatened he feels, the more he reads ordinary details as signals that he is unsafe. Before he feels comfortable anywhere, he scans for escape routes, noting doors, side halls, parking lots, and the quickest way back to his car. He frequently looks behind him when he walks, a habit that has followed him into shopping centers, office buildings, and even the hallways outside his own apartment. He tells himself he is being practical, but the vigilance is driven by the conviction that he has already missed the signs once and cannot afford to do so again. The more he sees himself as someone who somehow invited that violence, the more he treats the world as a place that must be preemptively managed. That belief has made his life smaller and more solitary; he keeps to familiar routes, declines invitations, and sits with his back to walls when he can, all because he is certain that the wrong place, the wrong angle, the wrong person could make him vulnerable again.

Raúl's work as a tax consultant now unfolds under those same constraints. He has built his practice around a quiet home office, remote meetings, and a carefully controlled routine, because going to new client sites or unfamiliar conference spaces leaves him tense and watchful. Even there, a photograph in a file, a client describing an injury, or the sight of someone walking in with a bandaged hand can pull him back into the memory of being pinned to the ground. The body remembers before he can reason with it: his shoulders tighten, he checks the room, and he is already planning how to get out if needed. Once that happens, the old thought returns that he must be flawed in some fundamental way, because a man who cannot walk into a lobby without scanning for exits must be damaged or tainted. That self-judgment deepens his sense of isolation, and in quieter hours he broods over whether there is any real future left for him at all.

Over the months, Raúl found himself living in a tense, self-policing rhythm that has worn him down. He sleeps lightly, keeps his phone charged, and notices with embarrassment how often he studies the faces of people he passes, as if a threatening figure could appear from anywhere. The more he watches for danger, the more ordinary sights acquire a sharpness that startles him: a bruise on a cashier's cheek, a cyclist's scraped knee, the ache in his own shoulder when he reaches for a file. Each of these can jolt him back into the police encounter, and each jolt seems to confirm that he is not safe and cannot trust his own judgment. That in turn feeds the belief that he is cut off from other people, living behind an invisible barrier while everyone else moves through the city without the same dread. He finally sought help after avoiding a client meeting in an unfamiliar part of town and then spending the next evening staring at the ceiling, convinced that his life had become a narrow corridor of fear. What frightens Raúl most now is that he may never feel ordinary safety again; what he hopes for, though he can barely say it aloud, is to stop blaming himself and to walk through the world without constantly searching for the next place to run.

It describes threat as increasing vigilance and fear, but it does not explicitly show the sense of threat producing triggers/reminders or cueing stimuli.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Triggers → Negative Appraisals: The vignette shows triggers/reminders leading to intrusions and vigilance, but it does not clearly state that the triggers themselves drive negative appraisals in the same paragraph.
  e.g. "Every time she walked through that car park, the thought arrived with her: this is what your life is now — flinching at nothing."
  e.g. "Seeing a man in the same jacket made her think, with quiet certainty, that she would never stop being afraid."
  e.g. "The sound of raised voices next door told her, with a logic she couldn't argue with, that nowhere was ever really safe."
- Threat → Triggers: It describes threat as increasing vigilance and fear, but it does not explicitly show the sense of threat producing triggers/reminders or cueing stimuli.
  e.g. "Already running on threat, she found that almost anything could tip into a warning — a van parked at an odd angle, a light left on that shouldn't have been."
  e.g. "The background hum of danger she carried everywhere made ordinary cues feel like messages — each one confirming what her body already believed."
  e.g. "Living at that pitch of alertness, she found the world had become dense with reminders she couldn't stop reading."
